lessons.title: What happens when you visit a website
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Ordering a web page, like a pizza

When you visit a website, it feels instant. But behind the scenes, two computers have a quick conversation, a lot like ordering a pizza:

| Pizza | Website |
| --- | --- |
| You decide what you want | You type a web address, like `pbskids.org` |
| You look up the pizza shop's phone number | The browser asks a **DNS server** where that website lives |
| You call and place your order | The browser sends a **request** to the website's **server** |
| The shop delivers your pizza | The server sends back the page's files |
| You eat! | The browser reads the files and shows you the page |

All of that usually happens in less than a second!

### Who's who

- The **browser** (Chrome, Safari, Edge) is the app on *your* device that asks for pages and shows them.
- A **server** is a computer somewhere else that stores websites and sends them out when asked.
- **DNS** is like the internet's phone book: it turns a name like `pbskids.org` into the server's number.

### New words

- **Browser**: the app that shows you web pages.
- **Server**: a computer that sends out websites.
- **Request**: a message asking a server for something.
- **DNS** (*Domain Name System*): the internet's phone book.

lessons.title: What happens when you visit a website
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## From URL to pixels

Typing `https://example.com` and pressing Enter starts a chain of steps that usually finishes in under a second.

1. **Parse the URL.** The browser splits it into the protocol (`https`), the domain (`example.com`) and the path (`/`).
2. **DNS lookup.** Computers find each other by **IP address** (like `93.184.215.14`), not by name. The browser asks a **DNS** (Domain Name System) resolver to translate the domain into an IP address. Answers are cached, so repeat visits skip most of this.
3. **Connect.** The browser opens a connection to that IP address. With `https`, it also negotiates **TLS** encryption, so nobody in between can read or alter the traffic.
4. **Request.** The browser sends an **HTTP request**, a short text message like `GET / HTTP/1.1` plus headers.
5. **Response.** The **server** answers with a **status code** (`200 OK`), headers, and a body: the HTML.
6. **More requests.** The HTML links to CSS, JavaScript and images, and the browser requests each one. A typical page makes dozens of requests.
7. **Render.** The browser builds the DOM from the HTML, applies the CSS, runs the JavaScript and paints pixels.

### Client and server

The browser is the **client**: it asks. The **server** is a program (and the machine running it) that answers. The same pattern holds when an app talks to an API; you'll build both sides in the C# and React courses.

### New words

- **IP address** (*Internet Protocol address*): the numeric address of a device on a network.
- **DNS** (*Domain Name System*): the system that maps domain names to IP addresses.
- **TLS** (*Transport Layer Security*): the encryption behind the lock icon and `https`.
- **Client**: the side that makes requests.
- **Render**: turn HTML, CSS and JavaScript into what you see.

lessons.title: Web addresses
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## A web address is like a home address

A home address has parts: a street, a city, a country. A web address, called a **URL**, has parts too:

```
https://www.pbskids.org/games/dino
```

| Part | In our example | What it means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Protocol** | `https` | *How* to talk to the server. The **s** means **secure**: nobody can snoop. |
| **Domain** | `www.pbskids.org` | *Which* website. It's the website's name. |
| **Path** | `/games/dino` | *Which page* on that website, like a room number. |

The `://` after the protocol is just punctuation that separates it from the domain.

> Look for `https` and a lock icon in your browser's address bar before typing anything into a website.

### New words

- **URL** (*Uniform Resource Locator*): a web address.
- **Protocol**: the rules for how the browser and server talk.
- **Domain**: the website's name.
- **Path**: which page on the website.

lessons.title: URLs and domain names
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Anatomy of a URL

A **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) identifies a resource and how to reach it:

```
https://shop.example.com:443/games/puzzles?sort=new&page=2#reviews
└─┬─┘   └┬─┘ └────┬────┘ └┬┘└─────┬─────┘ └──────┬──────┘ └──┬──┘
scheme  sub    domain    port    path         query       fragment
```

| Part | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| **Scheme** (`https`) | The protocol. `https` is HTTP over TLS (encrypted). |
| **Host** (`shop.example.com`) | The server. `example.com` is the registered **domain**; `shop` is a **subdomain** the owner controls; `.com` is the **top-level domain** (TLD). |
| **Port** (`:443`) | Which "door" on the server. Usually omitted: `https` defaults to 443 and `http` to 80. |
| **Path** (`/games/puzzles`) | Which resource on that server. |
| **Query string** (`?sort=new&page=2`) | Parameters as `key=value` pairs, separated by `&`. Servers use them for search, filters and pagination. |
| **Fragment** (`#reviews`) | A spot within the page. It's never sent to the server; the browser uses it to scroll. |

### Domains and DNS

Owners register a domain through a **registrar**. DNS records then point names at servers: an **A record** maps a name to an IPv4 address, and a **CNAME** points a name at another name.

### Escaping

Some characters are special in URLs (`?`, `&`, `#`, spaces), so values are **percent-encoded**: a space becomes `%20`. In HTML, a literal `&` should be written `&`.

### New words

- **Subdomain**: a name to the left of the domain, like `shop` in `shop.example.com`.
- **Port**: a number that selects a service on a server.
- **Query string**: `key=value` parameters after `?`.
- **Fragment**: the part after `#`, used only by the browser.

lessons.title: The server's reply card
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Requests and replies

When your browser asks a server for a page, that message is called a **request**. The server always answers with a **response**, and every response comes with a number called a **status code**: a quick way of saying how things went.

The language they use to talk is called **HTTP**.

### The three codes you'll see most

| Code | Means | Pizza version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **200** | OK! Here's your page. | Here's your pizza! |
| **404** | Not found. That page doesn't exist. | We don't have that pizza. |
| **500** | The server had a problem. | Our oven broke! |

You've probably seen a "404 Not Found" page when a link was broken. Now you know it's the server saying "I looked, but there's nothing there!"

### New words

- **HTTP** (*HyperText Transfer Protocol*): the language browsers and servers use to talk.
- **Response**: the server's answer to a request.
- **Status code**: a number in the response that says how it went.

lessons.title: HTTP requests, responses and status codes
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## HTTP: requests and responses

**HTTP** (HyperText Transfer Protocol) is a text-based, request/response protocol. Every exchange is one request and one response.

### A request

```http
GET /games/chess HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: text/html
```

- The **method** says what you want to do. `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `PUT` replaces, `DELETE` removes.
- The **path** is the resource.
- **Headers** add metadata (`Host`, `Accept`, cookies…).
- `POST` and `PUT` usually carry a **body**, such as form data or JSON.

### A response

```http
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html

<!DOCTYPE html>...
```

### Status code families

| Range | Family | Common codes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2xx | Success | `200 OK`, `201 Created`, `204 No Content` |
| 3xx | Redirection | `301 Moved Permanently`, `304 Not Modified` |
| 4xx | **Client** error (fix your request) | `400 Bad Request`, `401 Unauthorized` (not signed in), `403 Forbidden` (signed in, not allowed), `404 Not Found` |
| 5xx | **Server** error (the server broke) | `500 Internal Server Error`, `503 Service Unavailable` |

The first digit tells you who to blame: 4xx means the request was wrong; 5xx means the server failed. When you build the C# API later in the course, choosing the right status code is part of designing each endpoint.

### Stateless

HTTP is **stateless**: each request stands alone. Sites remember you between requests with **cookies**, small values the browser sends back on every request. (That's how this site keeps you signed in.)

### New words

- **Method**: the action a request asks for (GET, POST…).
- **Header**: a `Name: value` line of metadata.
- **Stateless**: each request is independent of the ones before it.
- **Cookie**: a small value the browser stores and sends back to a site.

lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Websites are made of files

A website is a bunch of **files** kept in **folders** on a server, just like files on a computer.

```
my-site/
├── index.html
├── images/
│   └── cat.png
└── pages/
    └── about.html
```

Folders are like drawers. `cat.png` is in the `images` drawer. `about.html` is in the `pages` drawer.

### Paths: directions to a file

To show a picture or link to a page, you give the browser **directions** from where your page is. These directions are called a **path**.

`index.html` sits in the main folder, so from there:

- the cat picture is in the `images` folder: `images/cat.png`
- the about page is in the `pages` folder: `pages/about.html`

The `/` means "go inside this folder".

### File names

- The part after the dot is the **file extension**: `.html` for pages, `.png` or `.jpg` for pictures, `.css` for styles.
- `index.html` is special: it's the page a server sends when you visit a folder.

### New words

- **Folder**: a place that holds files (and other folders).
- **Path**: directions to a file.
- **File extension**: the end of a file's name that says what kind of file it is.

lessons.title: Files, folders and relative paths
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Files, folders and paths

A static website is a folder tree that a web server exposes over HTTP. URL paths map onto it:

```
site/
├── index.html          → https://example.com/
├── css/site.css        → https://example.com/css/site.css
├── images/logo.png     → https://example.com/images/logo.png
└── pages/
    ├── team.html       → https://example.com/pages/team.html
    └── jobs.html       → https://example.com/pages/jobs.html
```

### Relative paths

A **relative path** is resolved from the folder of the current file.

| Path | From `pages/team.html`, resolves to |
| --- | --- |
| `jobs.html` | `pages/jobs.html` (same folder) |
| `./jobs.html` | `pages/jobs.html` (`.` = this folder) |
| `../index.html` | `index.html` (`..` = up one folder) |
| `../images/logo.png` | `images/logo.png` |

### Root-relative and absolute paths

- **Root-relative**: `/images/logo.png` starts at the site root, wherever the current page is. Convenient, but it breaks if the site is moved into a subfolder.
- **Absolute**: `https://example.com/images/logo.png` includes everything, so use it for other sites.

### Conventions that prevent pain

- Lowercase names with hyphens, no spaces: `team-photo.jpg`. Servers are often **case-sensitive**: `Logo.png` and `logo.png` are different files.
- `index.html` is the default document for a folder, so `/pages/` serves `pages/index.html`.

### New words

- **Relative path**: a path resolved from the current file's folder.
- **Root-relative path**: a path starting with `/`, resolved from the site root.
- **`..`**: the parent folder.

lessons.title: Your first web page from scratch
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## A production-ready page skeleton

Here's what a well-formed `index.html` contains before any content:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
    <meta name="description" content="One sentence for search results.">
    <title>Page title | Site name</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="css/site.css">
  </head>
  <body>
    <header>…</header>
    <main>…</main>
    <footer>…</footer>
  </body>
</html>
```

| Element | Why it's there |
| --- | --- |
| `<!DOCTYPE html>` | Standards mode. Without it, browsers emulate 1990s quirks. |
| `lang` | Pronunciation for screen readers, translation, spell-check. |
| `<meta charset="utf-8">` | Text encoding, so `é`, `ñ` and emoji display correctly. Put it first in `<head>`. |
| viewport `<meta>` | Responsive layout on phones (from the CSS course). |
| `description` `<meta>` | The snippet search engines usually show under your title. |
| `<title>` | Tab text, bookmarks, search results. Unique per page. |
| `<link rel="stylesheet">` | Your CSS. |
| Landmarks | `header`, `main`, `footer` for structure and accessibility. |

### Validating

The W3C Markup Validation Service (validator.w3.org) checks HTML against the standard. Browsers silently "fix" broken HTML, but they don't all fix it the same way, so valid markup behaves more predictably.

### New words

- **Standards mode**: the browser rendering mode triggered by the doctype.
- **Character encoding**: how bytes map to characters; UTF-8 (*Unicode Transformation Format, 8-bit*) covers every language and emoji.
- **Metadata**: data about the page, in `<head>`.
